checks.them: Okay, let's move on to some Android fundamentals. What happens when a child coroutine fails? When do you use SupervisorJob?

card.problem: Coroutine failure and SupervisorJob
card.adopted: none
card.heard: what happens when a child coroutine fails, when to use SupervisorJob
card.say: By default, a child failure cancels its parent and all the sibling coroutines. The exception goes up to the parent, and the parent cancels everything under it. I use SupervisorJob when one child's failure shouldn't stop the others. For example, a screen with several independent requests: one fails, the rest keep going. With a supervisorScope, the failure stays in that child, and I catch it there.

checks.them: StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel: which one for one-time UI events?

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events
card.adopted: none
card.heard: which one for one-time UI events
card.say: For one-time UI events, I'd use a Channel. A StateFlow always holds a value, so a new collector can get an old event again. A SharedFlow with replay zero can work too, but a Channel is simpler for events that should be handled once. The screen collects it in a lifecycle-aware way, so the event isn't lost when the screen is in the background.

checks.them: Why do we use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events
card.adopted: none
card.heard: why use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow
card.say: Because a screen can go to the background and come back. Without it, the collector keeps running in the background and wastes work. With repeatOnLifecycle, it starts when the screen is visible and stops when it isn't. So the UI only updates when someone can see it, and it starts again on return.

checks.them: Let's switch gears to some live coding. Write a function that takes a Flow of String of SSE text chunks and emits complete events. A chunk can cut an event anywhere.

card.problem: Live coding: turn a Flow of String SSE chunks into a Flow of complete events
card.adopted: Buffer the incoming text, split on the blank line between events, emit complete events and keep the leftover
card.heard: live coding: Flow of String SSE chunks to complete events
card.say: Okay, let's write it. I'll split the incoming text on the blank line between events, and keep any leftover piece in a buffer. Then I'll emit each complete event and carry the rest into the next chunk.
card.type: add@sseEvents: fun sseEvents(chunks: Flow<String>): Flow<String> = flow { ⏎     val buffer = StringBuilder() ⏎     chunks.collect { chunk -> ⏎         buffer.append(chunk) ⏎         while (true) { ⏎             val end = buffer.indexOf("\n\n") ⏎             if (end == -1) break ⏎             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) ⏎             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) ⏎             emit(event) ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }
card.then:
Next I'd handle the line ending, because some servers send 

 instead of 

.

transcript: Interviewer: The crash rate went down 90% at Debon. What was the hardest crash?
Candidate: The hardest one was a WebView crash.
Candidate: It only happened on certain phone models, so it was hard to reproduce.
Candidate: I got the device model and the page from Bugly, then tested on those phones.
Candidate: Most crashes were null pointers, out-of-memory errors and WebView problems.
Candidate: We fixed them group by group, starting with the most common.
Interviewer: Tell me about a device-specific bug. How did you find it?
Candidate: The device-specific one was a layout bug on small, cheap phones.
Candidate: A row of buttons overlapped on a narrow screen.
Candidate: I couldn't see it on my own phone, so I asked QA which models showed it.
Candidate: Then I opened the same screen on those phones and measured the width.
Candidate: The fix was to let the row wrap instead of squeezing.
Interviewer: Okay, let's move on to some Android fundamentals. What happens when a child coroutine fails? When do you use SupervisorJob?
Candidate: By default, a child failure cancels its parent and all the sibling coroutines.
Candidate: The exception goes up to the parent, and the parent cancels everything under it.
Candidate: I use SupervisorJob when one child's failure shouldn't stop the others.
Candidate: For example, a screen with several independent requests: one fails, the rest keep going.
Candidate: With a supervisorScope, the failure stays in that child, and I catch it there.
Interviewer: StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel: which one for one-time UI events?
Candidate: For one-time UI events, I'd use a Channel.
Candidate: A StateFlow always holds a value, so a new collector can get an old event again.
Candidate: A SharedFlow with replay zero can work too, but a Channel is simpler for events that should be handled once.
Candidate: The screen collects it in a lifecycle-aware way, so the event isn't lost when the screen is in the background.
Interviewer: Why do we use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?
Candidate: Because a screen can go to the background and come back.
Candidate: Without it, the collector keeps running in the background and wastes work.
Candidate: With repeatOnLifecycle, it starts when the screen is visible and stops when it isn't.
Candidate: So the UI only updates when someone can see it, and it starts again on return.
Interviewer: What survives process death? How do you restore the screen?
Candidate: Saved state survives process death, but only a small Bundle.
Candidate: The ViewModel does not survive it.
Candidate: So I'd keep the screen's input and scroll position in SavedStateHandle, and reload the rest from the database or network.
Candidate: On return, the ViewModel reads that saved state and rebuilds the screen.
Interviewer: Let's switch gears to some live coding. Write a function that takes a Flow of String of SSE text chunks and emits complete events. A chunk can cut an event anywhere.
Candidate: Okay, let's write it.
Candidate: I'll split the incoming text on the blank line between events, and keep any leftover piece in a buffer.
Candidate: Then I'll emit each complete event and carry the rest into the next chunk.

[board] fun sseEvents(chunks: Flow<String>): Flow<String> = flow { |     val buffer = StringBuilder() |     chunks.collect { chunk -> |         buffer.append(chunk) |         while (true) { |             val end = buffer.indexOf(" |  | ") |             if (end < 0) break |             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) |             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) |             emit(event) |         } |     } | }
Candidate: The code on the board already does the main job.
Candidate: One thing to add: the last event may have no blank line after it.
Candidate: When the stream ends, I'd emit whatever is left in the buffer, if it isn't empty.

[board] fun sseEvents(chunks: Flow<String>): Flow<String> = flow { |     val buffer = StringBuilder() |     chunks.collect { chunk -> |         buffer.append(chunk) |         while (true) { |             val end = buffer.indexOf(" |  | ") |             if (end < 0) break |             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) |             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) |             emit(event) |         } |     } | } |     if (buffer.isNotEmpty()) { |         emit(buffer.toString()) |         buffer.clear() |     }
Interviewer: How do you test it?
Candidate: I'd test it at three levels.
Candidate: First, small unit tests with chunks cut in bad places: in the middle of an event, in the middle of the blank line, and one event split across three chunks.
Candidate: Second, a test where the stream ends without a blank line, to check the last event still comes out.
Candidate: Third, a test with an empty chunk, which should emit nothing.
Candidate: I'd run them with runTest and collect the results into a list.
Interviewer: What if the server sends an event with no newline at the end?
Candidate: That's the case the flush already handles.
Candidate: When the stream ends, the leftover in the buffer is emitted as the last event.
Candidate: So an event with no blank line after it still comes out.
Candidate: The only thing I'd add is a check that the leftover isn't empty, so we don't emit a blank event.

[board] fun sseEvents(chunks: Flow<String>): Flow<String> = flow { |     val buffer = StringBuilder() |     chunks.collect { chunk -> |         buffer.append(chunk) |         while (true) { |             val end = buffer.indexOf(" |  | ") |             if (end < 0) break |             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) |             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) |             emit(event) |         } |     } | } |     if (buffer.isNotEmpty()) { |         emit(buffer.toString()) |         buffer.clear() |     }

Interviewer: Great. For the rest of the time, a new problem: design the Android app for ChatGPT. Users chat with the AI and see answers stream in. They can stop or regenerate an answer, upload a photo, use voice mode, and see their history on phone and web. Focus on the client. Tell me what you need from the backend.
Candidate: Got it.
Candidate: Before I design, let me confirm the scope.
Candidate: The client covers chat with streaming answers, stop and regenerate, photo upload, voice mode, and history on phone and web.
Candidate: I'll focus on the Android client and the backend contract.
Candidate: Out of scope for now: model training and the web client itself.
Interviewer: Let's keep text chat, streaming, stop and history as the core. Photo and voice come later. Draw the main layers of the app. Where does the data live?
Candidate: The data lives in a local database on the phone, and the repository is the only thing that writes to it.
Candidate: The UI never talks to the network directly.
Candidate: It observes the database through a Flow, so a message shows up the moment it's saved.
Candidate: The API client streams from the backend and hands each event to the repository.

[board] [Compose UI] --send--> [ViewModel] --> [Repository] --> [Local DB] |                                           | |                                           v |                                     [API client] --SSE--> backend | [Local DB] --Flow--> [ViewModel] --> [Compose UI]
Interviewer: What is your single source of truth?
Candidate: The local database is the single source of truth.
Candidate: The repository is the only writer, and the UI only reads from it through a Flow.
Candidate: The network never touches the UI directly, so a message shows up the moment it's saved.
Interviewer: How does the answer appear word by word? SSE, WebSocket, or polling? Why?
Candidate: SSE, because the answer only flows one way, from the server to the app.
Candidate: It runs over plain HTTP, so it's simple and it reconnects on its own.
Candidate: WebSocket is better when both sides send a lot, like voice mode later.
Candidate: Polling wastes requests and feels slow.
Interviewer: What does one event look like? Show me the format.
Candidate: Each event is a small block of text.
Candidate: The first line is `event: delta`, then `data:` with the JSON, then a blank line to end it.
Candidate: The JSON carries the message ID, the event ID and the text piece.
Candidate: The client uses the event ID to drop duplicates and to resume after a reconnect.

[board] [Compose UI] --send--> [ViewModel] --> [Repository] --> [Local DB] |                                           | |                                           v |                                     [API client] --SSE--> backend | [Local DB] --Flow--> [ViewModel] --> [Compose UI] | event: delta | id: 42 | data: {"messageId":"m1","seq":42,"text":"Hel"} |  | event: done | data: {"messageId":"m1","seq":43}
Interviewer: Tokens arrive 50 times a second. How do you update the UI without lag?
Candidate: I wouldn't update the UI on every token.
Candidate: I'd keep the growing text in the ViewModel and push it to the UI at a fixed rate, about every 50 to 100 milliseconds.
Candidate: Compose then recomposes once per update, not 50 times a second.
Candidate: The database still gets the full text, so nothing is lost.
Interviewer: Now voice mode, which we parked earlier. The AI is talking and the user starts talking. What happens?
Candidate: The user's voice should win.
Candidate: I'd stop the AI's speech right away and cancel its audio output.
Candidate: Then I'd switch to listening and send the new turn to the backend.
Candidate: The backend needs to support cancelling the current answer, so the old stream stops too.
Interviewer: A phone call comes in during voice mode. What happens?
Candidate: A phone call takes the audio focus, so the AI's speech stops and the mic goes quiet.
Candidate: I'd pause voice mode, not end it.
Candidate: When the call finishes, I'd ask the user before we start listening again.
Candidate: The backend keeps the turn open, so nothing is lost.
Interviewer: How do you know this feature works well in production? Which numbers do you watch?
Candidate: I'd watch three numbers.
Candidate: First, time to first visible token, and time to finish the answer.
Candidate: Second, the stop rate and the regenerate rate, because a high rate means the answer is wrong or slow.
Candidate: Third, crash-free rate and ANR rate, plus dropped frames while text streams in.
Candidate: I'd also track how many users come back the next day.
Interviewer: If you had only two weeks, what would you build first, and what would you cut?
Candidate: I'd build text chat with streaming first.
Candidate: Send a message, see the answer appear, and stop it.
Candidate: History comes with it, because every message is saved in the local database.
Candidate: I'd cut photo upload, voice mode, and regenerate.
Candidate: Regenerate is easy to add later, once the stream and the stop work well.
Interviewer: Okay, we're almost out of time. Do you have any questions for me?
Candidate: Yes, I have two.
Candidate: Six months after I join, what would make you feel you hired the right Android engineer?
Candidate: And what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, partial results, or reliable actions?
